summary: For 7–9 year-olds learning about minibeasts (insects, spiders, worms, snails, myriapods): these small invertebrates are the most numerous and diverse animals on Earth and do essential jobs — pollinating, decomposing, and feeding food chains. Core objectives: classify minibeasts by countable features (insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts; spiders/arachnids have 8 legs and 2 body parts; distinguish worms/snails/myriapods), use a simple branching classification key, and value minibeasts for their ecosystem roles. Best grounded in a real minibeast hunt with observed, sorted specimens, with on-screen sorting and keying as optional follow-on practice.
misconceptions: 'All minibeasts are insects' — spiders, worms, snails, woodlice and centipedes are NOT insects.
'A spider is an insect' — spiders are arachnids: 8 legs and 2 body parts, not 6 and 3.
'Minibeasts are pests / useless / dirty' — many are essential pollinators and decomposers that ecosystems depend on.
'Bugs are rare / only in special places' — invertebrates are the most numerous animals and live almost everywhere.
'All small crawly things are basically the same' — they fall into clearly different groups distinguished by countable features.

activities.title: Minibeast hunt and sort
steps: Go on a real minibeast hunt in the school grounds — look under logs, stones, leaves and paving slabs.
Before turning over one log or paving slab, predict how many minibeasts live underneath, then turn it over together and count what you find.
Collect or observe a set of specimens and group them by type (insects, spiders, worms, snails, woodlice, centipedes).
For each group, count the legs and body parts you can actually see and record them on a tally or sorting tray.
activities.insight: Minibeasts are not one blurry category but clearly different groups, and they are far more numerous and widespread than children expect — they live almost everywhere, even in the school grounds.

activities.title: Run the branching classification key
steps: Take each specimen (or a picture of one) and run it through a branching key of yes/no questions. Does it have legs? If yes: Six legs and three body parts (insect)? Eight legs and two body parts (arachnid, e.g. spider)? Fourteen legs and a body of hard plates (woodlouse)? Many more legs on a long body made of segments (myriapod: centipede or millipede)? If no legs: Tentacles on its head (snail or slug)? A long, soft body made of rings (worm)? Count the legs of adult minibeasts. Young insects such as caterpillars can look as if they have extra legs.
Follow the path the key takes until it lands on a group (insect, arachnid, woodlouse, worm, snail/slug, myriapod).
Explain why a spider (8 legs, 2 body parts) and a beetle (6 legs, 3 body parts) end up in different groups.
Build or complete your own short yes/no key that would separate two minibeasts you found.
activities.insight: Grouping is a rule you apply by checking shared, countable characteristics — a classification key turns sorting into a sequence of yes/no decisions rather than a guess.

activities.title: Give each minibeast its job
steps: Give each minibeast one or more ecosystem roles: pollinator (bees, butterflies), decomposer (worms, woodlice, some beetles), or prey/food for larger animals. Many minibeasts have more than one role.
Trace one example all the way through — e.g. with no bees, far fewer apple flowers get pollinated, so apple trees make much less fruit.
Follow a food chain: a robin eats worms and caterpillars — what happens to the robin if they're all gone?
Discuss or answer: name one job a minibeast does that helps plants, and give one reason minibeasts matter to a habitat.
activities.insight: These small, overlooked creatures are the ecosystem's essential workers — pollinating, breaking down dead material, and feeding other animals — so losing them would harm plants and the animals that depend on them.

activities.title: Check and sort: features and roles
steps: Sort a mixed set of minibeasts into groups (insect / arachnid / woodlouse / worm / snail or slug / myriapod).
Match each minibeast to its ecosystem job (pollinator, decomposer, prey).
Answer questions on leg and body-part counts, e.g. how many legs does a spider have? How many body parts does an insect have?

Answer the discriminating prompt: if every insect and minibeast disappeared overnight, and a friend says 'Good, they're just annoying pests, nothing would change,' do you agree? What might happen to plants and other animals?
activities.insight: You can reliably tell the groups apart by countable features and explain why each group matters — not just recognise a picture.

checkQuestion: Imagine every insect and minibeast — every bee, worm, beetle and woodlouse — disappeared overnight. A friend says 'Good, they're just annoying pests, nothing would change.' Do you agree? What might happen to plants and to other animals?
checkAnswer: Disagree — minibeasts do vital jobs. Bees and butterflies pollinate flowers, so many plants and crops could no longer make fruit or seeds; worms and woodlice break down dead leaves and return nutrients to the soil; and huge numbers of birds, frogs and other animals eat minibeasts, so they would go hungry. Losing them would harm plants and the animals that depend on them.
